portfolio.description: Student-centered budgeting concept focused on clear overviews, simple language, and approachable financial planning.
portfolio.title: budgIT – Student Budgeting App
portfolio.role: UX/UI Designer (Co-designed research, visual identity, and interactive prototyping)
portfolio.visuals: All visuals were made by me, including prototypes and final design.
portfolio.overview: budgIT is a budgeting and financial management concept designed specifically for university students. The project focused on understanding students’ real financial challenges and designing a user-friendly tool that helps with budgeting, expense tracking, savings goals, and financial awareness across both mobile and desktop platforms. The project was completed as part of a Human–Technology Interaction course and covered the full UX process: user research, conceptual design, information architecture, interaction design, and high-fidelity prototyping.
portfolio.problem: University students often struggle with managing finances due to irregular income (student aid, part-time jobs, loans), high fixed costs (rent, food), and lack of motivation or knowledge to plan finances in advance. User interviews revealed that most students rely on bank apps for passive tracking, but lack tools for proactive budgeting, clear overviews, and student-specific guidance. Existing financial apps were seen as too complex, not tailored to student life, or overwhelming to use.
portfolio.solution: We designed budgIT as a lightweight, student-centric financial hub focused on clarity, flexibility, and ease of use. The solution was shaped directly by user research and iterative design, ensuring that financial information is approachable rather than overwhelming. Design decisions prioritized clear overviews, simple language instead of financial jargon, and layouts that support quick understanding across both mobile and desktop contexts. I took main responsibility for building and visually polishing the interactive prototype, while collaborating closely with the team throughout all design phases.
portfolio.researchInsight: To ground the design in real student needs, we interviewed university students to understand their financial behaviors, pain points, and motivations. Insights from this research informed personas and usage scenarios that guided design and prioritization decisions.

keyTakeaways.text: Bank apps are used for monitoring, but proactive budgeting tools are missing.
Unpredictable earnings make planning and saving harder.
Motivation drops when financial products feel detailed or overwhelming.

portfolio.insightCallout: The persona kept design decisions anchored in real student constraints and goals.
portfolio.structureInteraction: We designed a dashboard-first information architecture where the primary navigation is organized around a high-level overview and clear feature groups, allowing users to access deeper details without cluttering the main view.

structureInteractionImage.alt: Information architecture diagram for the budgIT app

portfolio.outcome: The final result was a fully interactive prototype for mobile and desktop that clearly visualizes monthly budgets, expenses, and remaining funds, supports savings goals and basic financial learning, and adapts to different screen sizes and usage situations. Peer feedback highlighted the clarity, usability, and visual structure of the solution. The project demonstrated how user research can directly shape interaction design and lead to a more approachable financial tool for a specific user group.

persona.name: Persona 2
persona.goal: Manage finances clearly and save money without giving up student life.
frustrations: Budgeting apps not designed for students
persona.quote: I want to understand my finances quickly, without feeling restricted or overwhelmed.

beforeAfter.title: Before & After Navigation
beforeAfter.note: Side-by-side wireframe vs final UI highlighting icon-based navigation for accessibility and scannability.

portfolio.collaboration: We coordinated via Telegram for rapid feedback and divided responsibilities while keeping a shared vision.
impactLearnings: How to translate qualitative research into concrete UI decisions
How to design financial information without overwhelming users
The importance of iteration and content hierarchy in dashboards
Working in a multidisciplinary team with shared design ownership
portfolio.uxDecision: Based on user feedback, we moved charts above detailed lists to reduce cognitive load and help users quickly understand their financial situation.
portfolio.reflection: If continued, I would validate the design with usability testing and explore real-time data syncing across devices.

portfolio.title: AllTogether
portfolio.description: A single mobile experience that combines workouts, sleep, recovery, and nutrition into a clear daily overview.
portfolio.challenge: People who care about their health often use multiple apps and devices to track workouts, sleep, recovery, and nutrition. The result is fragmented data and poor overview - users know they are tracking, but not necessarily how they are doing. Our goal was to design a single mobile experience that brings this information together in a way that feels motivating, clear, and easy to understand at a glance.
portfolio.myRoleSummary: I worked as a UX/UI designer in a small team, contributing especially to:
myRolePoints: Defining the product vision and target users
Designing the mobile home screen focused on data clarity
Refining visual hierarchy, spacing, and UX writing
Evolving the design into a high-fidelity mobile UI
portfolio.userUnderstanding: We designed for 20-40-year-old health-conscious users who want to track their wellbeing without feeling overwhelmed by numbers or complex tools.
userDecisionAnchors: Showing insights instead of raw data
portfolio.visionSummary: Early on, we aligned on a clear vision: a mobile-first, all-in-one health app where users understand their daily status within seconds of opening the app.
visionPriorities: Modular content that can grow over time
Social features that feel supportive, not competitive
portfolio.wireframesSummary: We designed a simple navigation flow that always brings the user back to a clear overview. In the wireframing phase, we explored different dashboard layouts and tested how much information could be shown without overwhelming the user.
portfolio.wireframesInsight: Through iteration, it became clear that fewer, well-prioritized metrics worked better than dense data views.
finalExperiencePoints: Glanceable activity, sleep, and recovery data
Card-based layout for clarity and flexibility
Calm colors and increased white space
Familiar interaction patterns to reduce friction
Optional dark mode for real-world usage
portfolio.finalExperienceResult: The result is a mobile UI that feels informative but calm - something users can quickly check during everyday routines.
portfolio.outcome: The final concept delivers a cohesive mobile experience that combines fitness, nutrition, recovery, and social motivation into one interface. The project reinforced how much impact visual hierarchy, spacing, and prioritization have when designing data-heavy products.
portfolio.reflection: If continued, the next steps would include usability testing with real users and deeper validation of how users interpret the shown metrics.

portfolio.title: Airbnb - Usability study
portfolio.description: Usability evaluation of Airbnb's desktop experience focused on search, filters, navigation, and task success.
portfolio.role: UX Researcher (Expert review, lab observation, analysis)
portfolio.timeline: Evaluation Methods – Usability and User Experience
portfolio.tools: Expert Review, Usability Testing, Think-aloud, Task Scenarios, Post-test Interview
portfolio.overview: In this course project, we evaluated the usability of the Airbnb desktop website using established UX research methods. The goal was to identify usability issues affecting search, filtering, navigation, and overall user experience, and to assess how efficiently users can complete common accommodation-related tasks. The project combined individual expert review work with a moderated usability test conducted in a university usability lab.
portfolio.problem: Airbnb supports complex, multi-step search and booking behaviors, but desktop users can encounter friction when filtering, navigating, or interpreting system feedback. We needed to uncover the most impactful usability issues and understand where task flow breaks down.
portfolio.solution: We combined individual expert reviews with a moderated usability test in the university lab. My work included solo expert reviews, observing the lab test, analyzing the think-aloud video, and helping synthesize findings into severity-rated issues. Methods included task-based testing, observation and video analysis, post-test interviews and questionnaires, and severity analysis based on frequency and impact.
portfolio.outcome: Key focus areas included searching with constraints, modifying criteria, using and clearing filters, interpreting reviews and ratings, and moving between list and map views. We found poor discoverability of sorting and filtering, inconsistent filter behavior across views, unclear system feedback when filters were applied or removed, and user uncertainty about navigation state. A recurring insight was that users expected persistence and consistency in filters and became confused when the interface did not match those expectations.
impactLearnings: Apply UX research methods in a structured, academic setting
Conduct independent expert evaluations of complex digital products
Observe and analyze real user behavior objectively
Work with qualitative data such as think-aloud protocols and video recordings
Collaborate in a research team while maintaining clear individual responsibility
Translate observations into concrete usability insights
portfolio.reflection: Working as an observer and analyst strengthened my understanding of how small interaction design decisions can significantly affect user confidence and task efficiency. The combination of expert review and usability testing highlighted the importance of validating assumptions against real user behavior.
